text:
Predicates:
TwinOrTriplet(x) ::: x is a twin or triplet.
SpendsWithSiblings(x) ::: x spends a lot of time hanging out with and playing with siblings.
SameAgeSiblings(x, y) ::: x and y are siblings of the same age.
ComplainsAboutSiblings(x) ::: x complains often about annoying siblings.
LivesAtHomeRegularly(x) ::: x lives at home regularly.
DevelopsStrongBonds(x) ::: x develops strong bonds with family members.

Premises:
∀x (TwinOrTriplet(x) → SpendsWithSiblings(x)) ::: If people are twins or triplets, then they spend a lot of time hanging out with and playing with siblings.
∀x ∀y (SameAgeSiblings(x, y) → TwinOrTriplet(x)) ::: If people have siblings who are the same age, then they are twins or triplets.
∀x (ComplainsAboutSiblings(x) → ∃y (SameAgeSiblings(x, y))) ::: If people complain often about annoying siblings, then they have siblings who are the same age.
∀x (¬LivesAtHomeRegularly(x) → ¬DevelopsStrongBonds(x)) ::: If people do not live at home regularly, then they do not develop strong bonds with family members.
∀x (SpendsWithSiblings(x) → ¬LivesAtHomeRegularly(x)) ::: If people spend a lot of time hanging out with and playing with siblings, then they often did not live at home regularly.
Luke is both a twin or triplet and develops strong bonds with his family members, or he neither is a twin or triplet nor develops strong bonds with his family members: 
(TwinOrTriplet(Luke) ∧ DevelopsStrongBonds(Luke)) ∨ (¬TwinOrTriplet(Luke) ∧ ¬DevelopsStrongBonds(Luke)).

Conclusion:
SpendsWithSiblings(Luke)
